bibl.title: Attention and Implicit Memory: Priming-Induced Benefits and Costs Have Distinct Attentional Requirements

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: existence
span.quote: Experiment 1 shows that the costs, but not the benefits, are eliminated by division of attention at encoding.

span.label: priming-induced performance costs and benefits in picture naming
span.quote: The present study examined the effect of divided attention on priming-induced performance costs and benefits in a speeded picture-naming task.

span.label: behavioural-experiment
span.quote: In the implicit memory task, attention at encoding (full vs. divided) was manipulated between groups, and study condition (old vs. new vs. lure) was manipulated within groups.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: A lure picture activates the perceptually similar studied item as a competing incorrect response alongside the correct one, so naming requires selection among alternatives.
span.quote: By contrast, the lure condition (which elicits the cost) resembles production priming tasks in that it entails response competition at test: Because participants have studied a picture that is perceptually similar to the test cue, it is likely that the test cue elicits activation of that (incorrect) response, as well as the correct (but unstudied) response, requiring participants to select a response from these alternatives.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Because only the cost involves response competition at test, only the cost depends on attention at encoding, in line with the identification-production account.
span.quote: Thus, the absence of an attentional effect for the benefit, and the presence of such an effect for the cost, may be linked to the absence or presence of response competition at test, respectively, in accord with the identification-production account.

span.label: The small amnesic sample forced a within-subject design in Experiment 2, unlike the between-subjects design of Experiment 1.
span.quote: First, due to the limited number of amnesic participants, it was not feasible to employ a between-subjects design for the implicit and explicit memory tasks as we had in Experiment 1.

span.label: Amnesic participants' longer and more variable RTs complicate the between-group comparison, requiring z-score transformation.
span.quote: Because this difference complicates the comparison between groups regarding the effect of the manipulation of interest ( Faust, Balota, Spieler, & Ferraro, 1999 ), we converted RT scores to z-scores by using the group-specific mean and standard deviation of RTs in the new condition as the referent.

span.label: costs
span.quote: Experiment 1 shows that the costs, but not the benefits, are eliminated by division of attention at encoding. Experiment 2 shows that the costs (as well as the benefits) in this task are intact in amnesic participants, demonstrating that the elimination of the cost in the divided attention condition in Experiment 1 was not an artifact of the reduced availability of explicit memory in that condition

span.label: benefits
span.quote: Experiment 1 shows that the costs, but not the benefits, are eliminated by division of attention at encoding. Experiment 2 shows that the costs (as well as the benefits) in this task are intact in amnesic participants, demonstrating that the elimination of the cost in the divided attention condition in Experiment 1 was not an artifact of the reduced availability of explicit memory in that condition

span.label: divided attention
span.quote: Experiment 1 shows that the costs, but not the benefits, are eliminated by division of attention at encoding. Experiment 2 shows that the costs (as well as the benefits) in this task are intact in amnesic participants, demonstrating that the elimination of the cost in the divided attention condition in Experiment 1 was not an artifact of the reduced availability of explicit memory in that condition

span.label: response competition
span.quote: By contrast, the lure condition (which elicits the cost) resembles production priming tasks in that it entails response competition at test: Because participants have studied a picture that is perceptually similar to the test cue, it is likely that the test cue elicits activation of that (incorrect) response, as well as the correct (but unstudied) response, requiring participants to select a response from these alternatives

span.label: implicit memory
span.quote: Attention at encoding plays a critical and ubiquitous role in explicit memory performance, but its role in implicit memory performance (i.e., priming) is more variable: Some, but not all, priming effects are reduced by division of attention at encoding

span.label: PRIMING WITH THE SIGN REVERSED, and a field-level gap named in the abstract: the literature has focused EXCLUSIVELY on priming effects that are beneficial and has OVERLOOKED those that are costly, `wherein performance is harmed by prior exposure to task stimuli`. Nearly every other priming record in this corpus reports a facilitation. If `priming` is defined as an influence of prior exposure rather than as a benefit, then half the phenomenon has gone unstudied because of what the word suggests
span.quote: This work, however, has focused exclusively on priming effects that are beneficial in nature (wherein performance is enhanced by prior exposure to task stimuli), and has overlooked priming effects that are costly in nature (wherein performance is harmed by prior exposure to task stimuli)

span.label: cost and benefit as a SYMMETRIC PAIR of operationalisations - both are response times against the same NEW baseline, in the same task, from the same study phase: benefit = faster to OLD than to new, cost = slower to LURE than to new. Because the two share a baseline and differ only in the relation between studied and test item (identical versus merely similar), a dissociation between them cannot be explained by task or by measure
span.quote: The performance benefit in this task is manifested as faster response times in the test phase to old than to new pictures, and the cost as slower response times to lure than to new pictures

span.label: the amnesia control, and it is chosen for the ALTERNATIVE IT KILLS. Dividing attention damages explicit memory as well, so eliminating the cost that way leaves open that the cost was explicit all along. Amnesic participants have no explicit memory to lose and the costs are INTACT - so the Experiment 1 result cannot be an artifact of reduced explicit memory. A population used as a control condition rather than as a subject of study
span.quote: Experiment 2 shows that the costs (as well as the benefits) in this task are intact in amnesic participants, demonstrating that the elimination of the cost in the divided attention condition in Experiment 1 was not an artifact of the reduced availability of explicit memory in that condition

span.label: attention required WHERE A SELECTION MUST BE MADE - the paper's account of why one effect needs attention and the other does not is not about strength or depth but about whether the test cue leaves a CHOICE. The lure activates a wrong response alongside the right one; the old item points at a single correct response. Offered as a suggestion (`We suggest`, `may be linked`), and weighted here as one
span.quote: Thus, the absence of an attentional effect for the benefit, and the presence of such an effect for the cost, may be linked to the absence or presence of response competition at test, respectively, in accord with the identification-production account

span.label: contradicts → unitary-source accounts of priming costs and benefits (Rouder, Ratcliff & McKoon, 2000; Marsolek, 2008)
span.quote: The present finding that costs and benefits in priming are differentially affected by divided attention therefore poses a challenge to both theories insofar as it suggests that the source of these two effects, or the process by which they are manifested, is not identical.

span.label: replicates → Gabrieli et al. (1999) on divided attention not reducing the picture-naming priming benefit
span.quote: This aspect of our results is consistent with prior findings in a picture-naming task ( Gabrieli, et al., 1999 ).

span.label: replicates → Cave & Squire (1992) and Verfaellie et al. (1996) on normal picture-naming priming benefits in amnesia
span.quote: Prior studies have shown that the priming-induced performance benefit in picture naming is normal in amnesia ( Cave & Squire, 1992 ; Verfaellie, Gabrieli, Vaidya, Croce, & Reminger, 1996 ), and we expected to replicate that finding in Experiment 2.

span.label: costs —distinct-from→ benefits
span.note: differs in: WHETHER ATTENTION AT ENCODING IS REQUIRED - dividing attention eliminates the cost and leaves the benefit intact. Same task, same study phase, same participants, so the difference cannot be attributed to materials or measure · strength of the relation: 0.95 — THE RESULT. Two effects that a corpus would file under one word, separated by an experimental manipulation rather than by definition. Confidence 0.95 - this is the paper's own headline, stated in its abstract, not my reading of a discussion.
span.quote: Experiment 1 shows that the costs, but not the benefits, are eliminated by division of attention at encoding. Experiment 2 shows that the costs (as well as the benefits) in this task are intact in amnesic participants, demonstrating that the elimination of the cost in the divided attention condition in Experiment 1 was not an artifact of the reduced availability of explicit memory in that condition

span.label: divided attention —causes→ costs
span.note: direction on the measure: eliminates · strength of the relation: 0.9 — `eliminated`, not reduced - the paper's own word, and the vocabulary has the exact term for it. Experiment 2 is what licenses reading this as a fact about the cost rather than about explicit memory.
span.quote: Experiment 1 shows that the costs, but not the benefits, are eliminated by division of attention at encoding. Experiment 2 shows that the costs (as well as the benefits) in this task are intact in amnesic participants, demonstrating that the elimination of the cost in the divided attention condition in Experiment 1 was not an artifact of the reduced availability of explicit memory in that condition

span.label: response competition —causes→ costs
span.note: direction on the measure: increases · strength of the relation: 0.7 — Weight 0.7, the lowest here, and the paper's hedges are the reason: `We suggest`, `may be linked`, `it is likely that`. The mechanism is an interpretation offered after the result, not something the experiments manipulated.
span.quote: We suggest that the differential role of attention in priming-induced performance costs and benefits is linked to differences in response competition associated with these effects

span.label: ANOVA
span.quote: We submitted the data from these conditions to a 2-way mixed factorial ANOVA with a between-group factor of attention (full vs. divided) and a within-group factor of study condition (old vs. new).

span.label: t-test
span.quote: All t -tests were one-tailed because of the directional nature of the predicted effects.

span.label: power analysis
span.quote: Using the data from the full attention condition, we conducted a power analysis and determined that 52 participants would be required to have power of .80 to detect a cost in the divided-attention condition of the magnitude observed in the full-attention condition.

span.label: effect size
span.quote: Follow-up t -tests indicated that the cost was significant in the full attention condition, t (53) = 2.12, p = .02, d = .24, but not in the divided attention condition, p = .12.

span.label: partial eta squared
span.quote: Although the main effect of study condition was not significant ( p = .39), there was an interaction between attention and study condition, F (1, 106) = 5.68, p = .019, η p 2 = .051.

span.label: standard deviation
span.quote: To eliminate outliers in this final data set, trials that elicited RTs more than 2 SD above the participant’s mean in a given condition were excluded.

span.label: z-score standardization
span.quote: Because this difference complicates the comparison between groups regarding the effect of the manipulation of interest ( Faust, Balota, Spieler, & Ferraro, 1999 ), we converted RT scores to z-scores by using the group-specific mean and standard deviation of RTs in the new condition as the referent.

span.label: Dividing attention at encoding wiped out the priming-induced cost in speeded picture naming while leaving the priming-induced benefit untouched.
span.quote: In Experiment 1, we found that the benefits and costs associated with priming in a speeded picture-naming task are dissociably affected by division of attention at encoding: Whereas the benefit was unaffected by division of attention, the cost was eliminated by division of attention.

span.label: Amnesic patients showed both a normal benefit and a normal cost despite severely impaired explicit memory, ruling out the explanation that the cost is an explicit-memory artifact.
span.quote: Critically, the performance cost was also normal in the amnesic group despite an impairment in explicit memory comparable to that produced by divided attention in Experiment 1.

span.label: Costs and benefits in this task therefore arise from at least two separable implicit-memory mechanisms with different attentional requirements.
span.quote: The present findings indicate that priming-induced costs and benefits in a picture-naming priming task are the product of at least two distinct mechanisms, one that is attention-dependent and mediates the cost, and another that is independent of attention and mediates the benefit.

span.label: The dissociation is a problem for existing unitary-source models of priming costs and benefits (decision-node weighting and superimpositional representation accounts).
span.quote: Thus, neither theory apparently predicts or explains a dissociation between benefits and costs in priming.

span.label: priming (implicit memory)
span.quote: An important distinction may be drawn between explicit memory tasks, in which information from a prior experience is deliberately and consciously retrieved from memory (exemplified in the studies cited above), and implicit memory tasks, in which information from a prior experience influences subsequent behavior in the absence of deliberate retrieval from memory, a phenomenon termed “priming” ( Roediger & McDermott, 1993 ; Schacter, 1987 ).

span.label: priming-induced performance cost
span.quote: Performance costs are evident when one is asked to identify or generate words or objects that are similar but not identical to studied items.

span.label: benefit and cost in the speeded picture-naming task
span.term: benefit and cost in the speeded picture-naming task
span.quote: The performance benefit in this task is manifested as faster response times in the test phase to old than to new pictures, and the cost as slower response times to lure than to new pictures ( Ratcliff & McKoon, 1996 ; Rouder, et al., 2000 ).

span.label: identification-production distinction
span.quote: By this account, the critical distinction between priming effects that do or do not require attention at encoding is whether the test stimulus activates a number of possible responses from which one must be chosen (as in production tasks), or guides the participant to a single correct response (as in identification tasks), with divided attention at encoding having a greater effect on priming in production than in identification tasks.

span.label: attention at encoding (full vs. divided)
span.quote: In the implicit memory task, attention at encoding (full vs. divided) was manipulated between groups, and study condition (old vs. new vs. lure) was manipulated within groups.

span.label: study condition of the test picture (old vs. new vs. lure)
span.term: study condition of the test picture (old vs. new vs. lure)
span.quote: In the implicit memory task, attention at encoding (full vs. divided) was manipulated between groups, and study condition (old vs. new vs. lure) was manipulated within groups.

span.label: participant group (amnesic vs. control) in Experiment 2
span.term: participant group (amnesic vs. control) in Experiment 2
span.quote: The amnesic group consisted of 11 participants (three women) with etiologies including anoxia (n = 6), anoxia and left temporal lobectomy (n = 1), encephalitis (n = 3), and bithalamic stroke (n = 1).

span.label: response time to name the test picture
span.term: response time to name the test picture
span.quote: For each participant, we calculated the mean RT to identify pictures in the old, new, and lure conditions.

span.label: corrected recognition (hits minus false alarms) on the explicit memory test
span.term: corrected recognition (hits minus false alarms) on the explicit memory test
span.quote: Corrected recognition was higher in the full- than in the divided-attention group, t (46) = 2.18, p = .018, d = .60.

span.label: control group matched on age, education and WAIS-III Verbal IQ
span.term: control group matched on age, education and WAIS-III Verbal IQ
span.quote: The control group included 15 healthy participants (12 women) and was matched to the amnesic group in terms of age (mean = 61.0 years), education (mean = 15.3 years), and WAIS-III Verbal IQ (mean = 107.5; all p ’s > .30).

span.label: F (1, 106) = 82.44, p < .001 — overall priming benefit (old vs. new pictures) in Experiment 1
span.quote: Overall, there was a significant benefit, F (1, 106) = 82.44, p < .001, η p 2 = 44.

span.label: t (53) = 2.12, p = .02, d = .24 — the priming-induced cost, significant only under full attention (p = .12 under divided attention)
span.quote: Follow-up t -tests indicated that the cost was significant in the full attention condition, t (53) = 2.12, p = .02, d = .24, but not in the divided attention condition, p = .12.

span.label: F (1, 106) = 5.68, p = .019 — attention x study condition interaction showing the cost differed between full and divided attention
span.quote: Although the main effect of study condition was not significant ( p = .39), there was an interaction between attention and study condition, F (1, 106) = 5.68, p = .019, η p 2 = .051.

span.label: 132 msec / 89 msec — size of the priming benefit under divided versus full attention (numerically larger under divided attention)
span.quote: The interaction between attention and study condition showed a trend toward significance F (1, 106) = 3.12, p = .08, η p 2 = .03, but this effect reflected a numerically larger benefit in the divided-attention condition (132 msec) than in the full-attention condition (89 msec).

span.label: t (22) = 5.09, p < .001, d = 2.16 — impairment of corrected recognition in the amnesic group relative to controls in Experiment 2
span.quote: Corrected recognition was impaired in the amnesic group, t (22) = 5.09, p < .001, d = 2.16.

span.label: F (1, 24) = 4.22, p = .051 — the performance cost in Experiment 2, which did not differ between amnesic and control groups
span.quote: The cost was marginally significant, F (1, 24) = 4.22, p = .051, η p 2 = .149, and did not differ between the amnesic and control groups (group x study condition, p = .63).

span.label: 54 — participants per attention group in the Experiment 1 implicit memory task
span.quote: Therefore, in the implicit task, we included 54 participants in the full-attention and 54 in the divided attention condition.

span.label: 11 — amnesic participants tested in Experiment 2
span.quote: The amnesic group consisted of 11 participants (three women) with etiologies including anoxia (n = 6), anoxia and left temporal lobectomy (n = 1), encephalitis (n = 3), and bithalamic stroke (n = 1).
